title: Simple Cubic Equations

findings.finding: The topic has no opening review of undoing whole signed coefficients and carrying out signed division, both used directly in the second worked example.
findings.breakdown: To isolate x³ in −2x³=16, students must choose division by −2 and calculate 16÷(−2). These substantial prior skills are not rehearsed before the new cube-root step.
findings.checked: All supplied teaching was checked. There is no opening review or preceding topic; p3-information states that students should isolate x³ but does not rehearse these prior skills.
findings.assumptions: Linear-equation inverse operations and signed arithmetic are prior knowledge. The teacher checks the review and responds to gaps. This finding does not depend on calculator availability.

repair.proposal: Before p3-information, insert: (a) Calculate 18÷(−3). (b) Calculate (−24)÷(−6). (c) Solve 5u=35. (d) Solve −2v=18. Answers: −6; 4; u=7; v=−9. These four short items fit a one-page opening review.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse signed division and undoing positive and negative whole coefficients before the cubic examples.

findings.finding: Add a controlled comparison showing how the coefficient and constant together determine the solution’s sign.
findings.breakdown: The existing practice includes different sign combinations but no consecutive run holding magnitudes fixed while changing one sign at a time.
findings.checked: The proposed solutions are correct. Each transition in the four-part run changes only one sign. The unpatterned follow-up has solution x=−4. All methods are available from the worked examples.
findings.assumptions: Append these as further parts under p4-q1’s existing solving instruction.

repair.proposal: After p4-q1-f, add the single instruction ‘Predict the sign of each solution before solving.’ Add further parts: 2x³=54 [x=3]; 2x³=−54 [x=−3]; −2x³=−54 [x=3]; −2x³=54 [x=−3]. Follow with 5x³=−320 [x=−4]. In the run, magnitudes and equation structure stay fixed while one sign changes at a time.

findings.doneWhen: The optional run and unpatterned follow-up appear together under the existing question instruction.

findings.finding: Extend the existing container problem to connect doubling a cube’s side length with multiplying its volume by eight.
findings.breakdown: This numerical follow-up develops the cubic relationship using the same three containers and their original total volume.
findings.checked: Each original cube has volume 6 m³. Doubling its side gives volume (2∛6)³=48 m³, so three new cubes total 144 m³, eight times the original volume. Students can also compare cubes of numerical side lengths using the volume formula established in p4-q2-a; no general proof or new solving method is required.
findings.assumptions: The parts are optional follow-ups immediately after p4-q2-b.

repair.proposal: Add (c) ‘Each of the three containers is replaced by a cube whose side length is twice as long. What is the total volume of the three new containers?’ [144 m³.] Add (d) ‘By what factor has their total volume increased?’ [8.]

findings.doneWhen: The two optional numerical follow-up parts and their expected answers are appended to p4-q2.

findings.finding: The teaching does not demonstrate a non-perfect cube root as a finished exact answer, although exact form is explicitly required in p4-q2-b.
findings.breakdown: Every worked and guided example has an integer solution. The intermediate cube-root expressions are always evaluated, leaving students without a model of when to retain the root or how its exact value differs from a decimal approximation.
findings.checked: All teaching and practice were checked. The examples show cube-root notation, but none retains a non-perfect cube root as the final answer. The rounding instruction in p4-q1 does not explain exact form.
findings.assumptions: A scientific calculator is available, inferred from the requested decimal approximations. Calculator operation and rounding themselves are not missing prerequisites.

repair.proposal: Append a short worked variant to p3-example-group: ‘2x³=10; x³=5; x=∛5 exactly; x≈1.71 to 2 d.p. Since 5 is not a perfect cube, retain ∛5 for an exact answer; the decimal is an approximation.’

findings.doneWhen: Before independent practice, a worked variant models a non-perfect cube root as a finished exact answer and distinguishes it from its approximation.

importReview: Lean content review table: 7 of 7 blocks passed.
